title: Crushing It!: How Great Entrepreneurs Build Their Business and Influence—and How You Can, Too
author: Gary Vaynerchuk
summary:
*Crushing It!* is Gary Vaynerchuk's 2018 follow-up to his earlier book *Crush It!*, revisiting its central thesis roughly a decade later with updated platform guidance and dozens of real success stories from people who built businesses or brands using the original book's advice. The core argument hasn't changed: anyone, in any niche or industry, can build a meaningful personal brand and business by authentically documenting their expertise or passion on social media, and the explosion of platforms since the first book (Instagram, YouTube, podcasting, Facebook video, and others) has only multiplied the number of viable paths to do so.

Vaynerchuk's central distinction is between "documenting" and "creating" — he argues most people overestimate the polish and originality required to build an audience, when in fact simply documenting one's actual work, process, and expertise consistently over time is both more sustainable and more authentic than trying to manufacture original "content" from nothing. This lowers the barrier to entry considerably: the book is built around the premise that expertise or passion in almost any niche — however narrow — combined with consistent, platform-appropriate documentation, can build a loyal audience, which can then be converted into a business through products, services, sponsorships, or attention that supports an existing business.

A large portion of the book is organized platform-by-platform (Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, Snapchat, podcasting, and others as they existed at the time of writing), with Vaynerchuk offering specific tactical guidance for each — content formats that perform well, posting frequency, how each platform's algorithm and audience behavior differs, and case studies of people (often ordinary individuals rather than existing celebrities) who used that specific platform to build a following in their particular niche. This platform-specific granularity is paired with dozens of first-person success stories, interspersed throughout, of people from very different backgrounds and niches — food, real estate, comedy, parenting, fitness, and more — who applied the book's principles.

Running underneath the tactical platform advice is Vaynerchuk's consistent emphasis on patience, hustle, and self-awareness: he repeatedly warns readers against expecting overnight results, insists that most people quit too early because they don't accept the multi-year timeline real audience-building requires, and stresses "self-awareness" — an honest read of one's own strengths, weaknesses, and market position — as more important than any specific platform tactic. The book closes by reiterating that the fundamentals (authenticity, patience, hard work, and genuine value to an audience) matter more than which platform or tactic is currently trending, since platforms will keep changing while these fundamentals won't.

sections.title: Why Crushing It Still Matters
sections.summary:
This opening chapter reframes the argument from the original *Crush It!* for the current platform landscape, arguing that the explosion of new social platforms since the first book has made the underlying opportunity even bigger, not smaller or more saturated as some might assume.

The chapter's substance addresses the common objection that "it's too late" to build an audience on any given platform, countering with the observation that new platforms and formats keep emerging, and that niche depth (rather than broad fame) is enough to build a sustainable business.

It closes by previewing the rest of the book's structure — platform-specific tactical chapters interspersed with real success stories — and reiterating the book's founding distinction between documenting and creating.
keyLessons: New platforms keep emerging, so "it's too late" is a persistent but usually false objection.
Niche depth, not broad fame, is sufficient to build a sustainable audience-based business.
Documenting one's actual work and expertise is more sustainable than manufacturing original content from nothing.

sections.title: Self-Awareness
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that an honest, sometimes uncomfortable assessment of one's own strengths, weaknesses, and current market position is more important to long-term success than any platform-specific tactic covered later in the book.

The substance includes Vaynerchuk's critique of people who chase trends or copy others' successful formats without an honest read of their own actual skills and interests, arguing this mismatch is a leading cause of quitting or burning out before results materialize.

The chapter closes by connecting self-awareness to patience: an accurate read of one's starting point makes the multi-year timeline of real audience-building feel realistic rather than discouraging.
keyLessons: Honest self-assessment of strengths and weaknesses outperforms copying trends or others' formats.
Mismatched effort — chasing what's not authentically yours — is a leading cause of early quitting.
Accurate self-awareness makes a realistic, multi-year timeline feel achievable rather than discouraging.

sections.title: Instagram
sections.summary:
This platform-specific chapter covers tactical guidance for building an audience on Instagram as of the book's writing — content formats, engagement tactics, and the platform's particular visual and community norms — paired with a first-person success story of someone who built a business primarily through the platform.

The substance emphasizes consistency and community engagement (responding to comments, engaging with others' content in one's niche) as more important than production polish, and covers how Instagram Stories specifically opened new, lower-friction content opportunities at the time.

The chapter closes by tying the platform-specific tactics back to the book's broader documenting philosophy, showing how the featured entrepreneur applied it concretely on this particular platform.
keyLessons: Consistency and genuine community engagement outperform production polish on Instagram.
Lower-friction formats (like Stories) can open opportunities that higher-effort formats miss.
Platform-specific tactics should still be applied through the book's broader documenting philosophy.

sections.title: YouTube
sections.summary:
This chapter covers YouTube-specific strategy, emphasizing the platform's suitability for long-form, searchable, evergreen content that can continue attracting an audience long after publication, unlike more ephemeral social feeds.

The substance includes guidance on video-specific production considerations, the value of consistency and a recognizable format for retention, and a featured success story illustrating how a niche expert built a substantial audience through patient, consistent uploading over years rather than a single viral breakout.

The chapter closes by reinforcing patience as the key differentiator on this platform in particular, given how much longer YouTube's growth curve typically takes compared to some other platforms.
keyLessons: YouTube content tends to have more evergreen, searchable value than content on more ephemeral platforms.
A recognizable, consistent format supports audience retention over time.
YouTube growth typically requires more patience than other platforms before results compound.

sections.title: Facebook
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses Facebook's particular dynamics at the time of writing — including its role in reaching an older or different demographic than platforms like Instagram or Snapchat, and its native video features.

The substance covers tactics for using Facebook groups and native video to build community and reach, along with a case study of an entrepreneur who used the platform to reach an audience under-served by other platforms.

The chapter closes by noting that platform choice should follow where a reader's specific target audience already spends time, rather than choosing a platform based on general popularity alone.
keyLessons: Platform choice should follow where your specific target audience already spends time, not general popularity.
Facebook groups and native video were highlighted as particularly effective community-building tools.
Different platforms reach meaningfully different demographics, which should inform platform selection.

sections.title: Twitter, Snapchat, Podcasting, and Other Platforms
sections.summary:
This chapter covers the remaining major platforms of the time more briskly, applying the same documenting-over-creating philosophy to each while noting their distinct strengths — Twitter for real-time engagement and conversation, Snapchat for younger-audience reach and authentic behind-the-scenes content, podcasting for long-form, intimate audio connection with an audience.

The substance includes brief case studies for several of these platforms, reinforcing that the specific tactics differ by platform but the underlying principles (consistency, authenticity, patience) remain constant across all of them.

The chapter closes by acknowledging that new platforms will continue to emerge after the book's publication, and that readers should apply the same underlying evaluation process to any new platform rather than needing platform-specific instructions from Vaynerchuk indefinitely.
keyLessons: Each platform has a distinct strength (real-time conversation, younger reach, intimate long-form audio) that should inform how it's used.
The underlying principles of consistency, authenticity, and patience remain constant across every platform covered.
Readers should be able to apply the book's evaluation process to future platforms not covered in the book itself.

sections.title: Legacy
sections.summary:
The closing chapter zooms out from platform tactics to the bigger-picture argument Vaynerchuk wants readers to leave with: that building a personal brand isn't just about short-term business results, but about building something durable — genuine expertise, relationships, and reputation — that outlasts any single platform's trends.

The chapter revisits the patience theme one final time, arguing that readers who treat this as a multi-year identity and legacy project, rather than a quick tactic for immediate income, are the ones who ultimately succeed by the book's own case studies.

The book closes with a direct call to action: start documenting now, in whatever niche and however imperfectly, rather than waiting for ideal conditions or a fully formed plan.
keyLessons: Personal branding is framed as a durable, multi-year legacy project, not a short-term tactic.
The book's own case studies suggest patience-oriented people, not those chasing quick tactics, ultimately succeed.
The practical takeaway is to start documenting immediately, imperfectly, rather than waiting for ideal conditions.
Document your actual work and expertise consistently rather than trying to manufacture original "content" from nothing.
Niche depth is sufficient to build a sustainable audience-based business — broad fame isn't required.
Honest self-awareness about your own strengths and weaknesses matters more than copying others' successful formats.
Choose platforms based on where your specific target audience already spends time, not general popularity.
Each platform has distinct strengths and norms; tactics should be adapted per platform even as underlying principles stay constant.
Consistency and genuine engagement typically outperform production polish, especially early on.
Most people quit too early because they underestimate the multi-year timeline real audience-building requires.
New platforms keep emerging, so "it's too late" is a persistent but usually false objection to starting.
Treat personal branding as a durable legacy project, not a short-term income tactic.
Start documenting immediately and imperfectly rather than waiting for a fully formed plan.

quotes.text: An entrepreneur is someone who finds a way.

The Internet is an entrepreneur's oyster, and you can use its pearly platforms to build a personal brand so powerful that the world is not only willing to pay you for your products or services or to promote other people's products and services, but also it might even be willing to pay you to just be you.
A strong personal brand is your ticket to complete personal and professional freedom.
You are unique, and you provide nuance, perspective, and details that no one else can.
Document, don't create.
Put your stuff up and see what the market has to say about it.
You just have to make the choice to actually do it. I am so tired of excuses.
You are not going to be successful unless you put the work in. If anybody tells you otherwise, they're full of shit.
It's one thing to read the book; it's another thing to take action.
There's no secret to being successful on the Internet. You need to be good at what you do; you need to be passionate about it and go crush it.
Success takes a shitload of work, and the people who ultimately break through and crush it are those who get all that and go for their dreams anyway.
If you really want to be like me, quit being a student of entrepreneurship and start doing the goddamn work.
I don't have second sight; I just have a lot more patience than you do.
Talent has little value without patience and persistence.
There was a time when Kobe and Beyoncé still had to use their last names.
You are the reason why you're not crushing it yet.
Short of self-destructive behavior or a complete lack of self-awareness, there is very, very little you can do that you cannot recover from.
You'll be amazed how quickly you can work when you're no longer tethered by the tyranny of other people's opinions.
Remember, you're only crushing it if you're living entirely on your own terms.
Your intent will be reflected in your authenticity.
When you really own it, and you put yourself out there and be you, your vibe is going to attract your tribe, and you're going to be able to make change in this world.
There's no point in trying to be an entrepreneur without passion.
What usually hamstrings entrepreneurs isn't merely the mistakes they make when executing their vision, but the mistakes they make before they even get started.
The quicker you realize that getting into this game for the gold is the quickest path to long-term failure, the better off you'll be.
Don't look for a nine-step program to success here, though. I can't give you one. The principles are universal; the path is all yours.
You should be plotting how to adapt your content to appeal to every platform your audience might visit in a given day.
If you're seeking to build your audience, go where the audience goes, wherever that may lead.
Facebook is the cost of entry to building a personal brand.
It pays to be brave.
Please, please, just try, if not for yourself, then for the people you love who are watching you and who want you to be happy.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Documenting vs. Creating
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Vaynerchuk's distinction between manufacturing original, highly polished "content" from scratch (creating) versus simply and consistently sharing one's actual work, process, and expertise as it happens (documenting) — the book's central, lower-barrier-to-entry approach to building an audience.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Self-Awareness (as a business skill)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: An honest, unflinching assessment of one's own actual strengths, weaknesses, and market position, which Vaynerchuk argues is more predictive of long-term success than any specific platform tactic, since it prevents wasted effort chasing trends that don't match one's real capabilities.

actionSteps: Pick one platform where your specific target audience already spends time (not just the most popular platform generally) and commit to posting there consistently for 90 days.
Instead of trying to create a polished, original piece of content this week, document one piece of your actual work or process as it happens and share it.

Write an honest, specific self-assessment of your current strengths and weaknesses relevant to your niche, and identify one mismatch between what you've been trying to do and what you're actually good at.
Study one successful account in your niche and identify specifically what platform-native tactic (not just general popularity) is driving their engagement.
Set a concrete, multi-year timeline expectation for your own audience-building effort, written down, so short-term slow progress doesn't trigger premature quitting.
reflectionQuestions: What genuine expertise or passion do you have that you've been hesitant to document because it doesn't feel "content-worthy" enough?
Where have you been chasing a trend or format that doesn't actually match your real strengths?
If you fully accepted that meaningful results might take years rather than months, what would you start doing differently today?

points: The book's dozens of individual success stories are inherently survivorship-biased — it profiles people for whom the strategy worked, without a comparable accounting of how many people applied similar tactics and didn't succeed, making it hard to assess the approach's actual success rate.

Vaynerchuk's own commercial interests (his agency VaynerMedia works with brands on exactly this kind of social media and influencer strategy) create a potential incentive to promote the viability of building a following via these platforms more broadly than pure disinterested analysis might support.

Platform-specific tactical advice in the book has aged unevenly since 2018 — several named platforms and features (Snapchat's relative prominence, specific Facebook and Instagram feature sets) have shifted substantially, meaning readers need to treat the platform chapters as historically illustrative rather than current tactical guidance.

The "anyone can build a following in any niche" framing understates the role of algorithmic changes, platform saturation in some niches, and paid advertising dynamics that have made organic audience-building meaningfully harder in many categories since the book's publication.

Critics of Vaynerchuk's broader body of work have noted a tendency toward hustle-culture framing that can read as dismissive of legitimate structural or personal constraints (health, caregiving responsibilities, financial precarity) that limit some readers' capacity for the sustained, years-long effort the book calls for.
criticalTake.contextNote: Because the book is explicitly platform-tactical, its specific guidance has aged the fastest of any part of the content — the underlying philosophy (documenting, patience, self-awareness) has held up better than the platform-by-platform tactical chapters, which reflect the social media landscape as it existed in 2018.

whoThisIsFor: Entrepreneurs, side-hustlers, and small business owners looking to build a personal brand or business through social media and content, especially those who feel they lack a "big enough" niche or story to be worth documenting.
whenToReadThis: When starting to build a personal brand or business around expertise or passion and needing both a mindset reset and concrete, platform-by-platform (if somewhat dated) tactical starting points.

authorBio.name: Gary Vaynerchuk
authorBio.bio:
Gary Vaynerchuk (often known as "Gary Vee") is a Belarusian-American entrepreneur, author, and media personality. He first built a public profile by growing his family's wine business, Wine Library, into a major e-commerce success partly through early and aggressive use of online video and social media, then pivoted to founding VaynerMedia, a digital and social media marketing agency.

Vaynerchuk has become one of the most prominent public voices on social media marketing, personal branding, and entrepreneurship, known for a high-energy, direct, and sometimes profanity-laced communication style across his own extensive content output on platforms including YouTube, Instagram, and podcasting.

*Crushing It!* (2018) followed his earlier book *Crush It!* (2009), revisiting and updating its core argument for the substantially changed social media landscape roughly a decade later, and became a New York Times bestseller in its own right.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on general knowledge of this well-known, widely reviewed book. Quotes are drawn from a small set of widely and consistently cited lines from the English original rather than the full requested count, to stay within safe excerpting limits.

---  ---  Quote retrofit pass round 8: Verified against the page-cited quote collection at bookey.app/book/crushing-it/quote (92-quote Goodreads work-quotes page at goodreads.com/work/quotes/57620167-crushing-it corroborates several of the same lines, e.g. 'Document, don't create'), cross-checked with targeted web searches for exact wording. Of the 5 pre-existing quotes, only 'Document, don't create.' could be re-verified as belonging to this book (Chapter 3, pages 141-177) and was kept. 'Legacy is greater than currency.' was dropped as contamination: it is confirmed via multiple sources (including a YouTube video explicitly titled 'Legacy is Greater Than Currency | Final Chapter | Crush It') to be the closing line of the EARLIER, DIFFERENT book Crush It! (2009), not Crushing It! (2018). 'Self-awareness is the ability to accurately perceive your own emotions, strengths, weaknesses, actions, and how they align with your standards.' was dropped because it could not be found in any real Crushing It source and closely mirrors a generic CASEL psychology definition of self-awareness, suggesting it was fabricated/paraphrased rather than an actual line from the book. 'Patience, in fact, might be the most overlooked ingredient in the recipe for success.' and 'There are no shortcuts. Anyone who's telling you there's a shortcut to your success, other than putting in the time, doesn't know what they're talking about.' were also dropped as unverifiable — no matching source could be located for either exact wording. 30 new quotes were added, sourced from the page-cited Chapter 1-16 quote listing (with page ranges spanning roughly pp.28-471 depending on edition) at bookey.app, omitting lines in that list that were actually spoken by featured entrepreneurs profiled in the book (e.g. Pat Flynn, Costa) rather than by Gary Vaynerchuk himself.
